beat_times.line: A guest book that knows who is coming. The lantern is lit.
I work the night desk at the Wayside Motel, out on Route 9, where the road runs between tw
Twelve rooms. Most nights, nobody comes.
The guest book sits open on the counter. The owner, Mr. Pell, likes ink. He says a name in
Every morning, when I hand over the keys, there's a new line in it. Room six. Signed at tw
Room six has been boarded up since before I was hired.
The first week, I blamed the day staff. The second week, I stopped blaming anyone. I start
Last night, at two thirteen, the lights in the parking lot flickered.
At two fourteen, the pen moved.
Not much. Just a roll. Like someone had brushed it with a sleeve.
I didn't look at the book. I looked at the camera. On the screen, I was sitting at the des
And behind me, close enough to breathe on my neck, a
man in a wet raincoat was leaning over my shoulder to write.
I didn't turn around. I couldn't.
When the lights came back, the office was empty.
The book was open. The ink was still wet.
Room six. Two fourteen a.m. And the name was mine.
Mr. Pell came in at six. He read the line very quietly.
Then he took a key off the hook. A key I had never seen.
"It's always the one at the desk," he said. "Your room's ready."

places.name: The Motel Office
places.design: A cramped, wood-paneled front office/reception room, stale and time-worn. Main colours are nicotine-stained beige and dark, varnished walnut. Behind the worn wooden counter is a back-wall board of dark-stained wood with rows of empty key hooks. Telling objects: an old black rotary-dial telephone on the left of the counter; a flat, leather-bound guest book always lying open in the centre; a heavy brass desk bell and a green-shaded banker's lamp with an old fabric cord to its right. The only night light sources are the lamp's dim, flickering sodium-yellow bulb and the cold blue glow from a phone screen. places.name: The Wayside Motel
places.design: A single-storey, cinder-block roadside motel, circa 1970, rundown and paint-peeled. The low flat roof has rusted metal trim. Outside: A row of identical dark green doors (number 6 is also nailed with weathered grey planks). The short walkway is lit by dim, candelabra-style yellow bulbs in old frosted glass sconces. Concrete steps lead from each door to the cracked asphalt parking lot and a two-lane blacktop road. Thick, silent fog blankets everything. Inside: Not shown for these scenes.

screening.hook: The opening line about the permanently boarded-up Room 6 establishes an immediate, intriguing horror mystery within the first five seconds.

notes.note: A young man is shown standing outside Room 6 while the female narrator introduces her routine at the empty motel. The unannounced character creates confusion about who we are following.
The red cursive text being written by the pen does not match the clean 'June Marsh' signature and timestamp revealed in the close-up at 1:26.
The wide shot revealing the wet raincoat figure leaning right behind her is creepy, but the completely static image lacks subtle movement like rain drip or breathing, making it feel less visceral.

scares.why: The sudden visual shift from her phone screen to the wide shot showing the entity hovering directly over her shoulder creates a chilling, claustrophobic reveal.
